question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) explained
direct_answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that objects of a subclass should be replaceable for objects of their superclass without breaking the program. If class B extends class A, anywhere you use an A object you should be able to use a B object and get the same correct behavior — no surprises, no exceptions.

sections.title: Understanding Behavioral Substitution
sections.content:
The **Liskov Substitution Principle** (LSP) is the L in SOLID. It says that a subclass must be usable wherever its parent class is expected, without causing errors or unexpected behavior. This goes beyond compile-time type safety — your code might compile fine, but if a subclass changes assumptions that calling code relies on, you've violated LSP.

Think of it like a power adapter: if you replace a US plug adapter with a European one, devices expecting a US adapter will fail even though both are "adapters." The principle is named after **Barbara Liskov**, who formalized it in 1987.

In Spring Boot apps, LSP violations often appear when you override service methods and silently change behavior — for example, a CachedOrderService that extends OrderService but doesn't actually save to the database, breaking callers who expect persistence.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Substitutability|~LSP core|subtype usable wherever base is|no surprises for callers
blue|Classic Break|~Square / Rectangle|setWidth changes height|the area assertion fails
emerald|Rules|~honor the contract|don't strengthen preconditions|don't weaken postconditions
violet|Symptom|~runtime surprise|child throws or no-ops where base works

sections.title: Classic Rectangle-Square LSP Violation
When LSP Matters Most
sections.content: Apply LSP thinking when designing service hierarchies in Spring Boot. If you have a **PaymentProcessor** interface with implementations like StripePaymentProcessor and PayPalPaymentProcessor, any code using PaymentProcessor must work identically with both — same error handling, same transaction guarantees, same idempotency behavior. LSP is critical in framework code: if you extend Spring's AbstractController and override methods, framework code calling those methods must still work. It's also vital in **repository patterns** — if you have CachedUserRepository extending DatabaseUserRepository, operations like save() and findById() must behave consistently, not skip the database or return stale data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inheritance based on real-world taxonomy**: Freshers see "Square is a Rectangle in math" and create that inheritance, ignoring that the behavioral contract (independent width/height) doesn't match.
- **Thinking compilation equals correctness**: If your Square subclass compiles when passed to a method expecting Rectangle, freshers assume LSP is satisfied — but runtime assertion failures or wrong calculations reveal the violation.
- **Overriding with narrower behavior**: Creating a ReadOnlyUserRepository that extends UserRepository but throws exceptions on save() — callers expecting UserRepository get runtime crashes. The compiler allows it, but it violates the substitution principle.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Behavioral substitution**: subclass must work anywhere parent is used, not just compile
**Precondition weakening**: subclass can accept more inputs than parent, never fewer
**Postcondition strengthening**: subclass can promise more guarantees, never fewer
**Invariant preservation**: properties that always hold for parent must hold for subclass
**Exception contracts**: subclass cannot throw new checked exceptions not in parent signature
**Side effects matter**: if parent method has no side effects, subclass override cannot add them
**Real-world is-a != OOP is-a**: mathematical or domain relationships don't always translate to inheritance

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The Liskov Substitution Principle says that if you have a subclass, you should be able to use it anywhere the parent class is expected without breaking anything. It's not just about the code compiling — it's about behavior. The classic example is Rectangle and Square. Mathematically, a square is a rectangle, so it seems natural to make Square extend Rectangle. But here's the problem: a Rectangle lets you set width and height independently. If you set width to five and height to four, you expect the area to be twenty. But if you pass in a Square instead, setting width also changes height because a square's sides must be equal. Now the area is sixteen, and your code breaks. That's an LSP violation. The compiler is happy, but the behavior is wrong. In a Spring Boot app, you might see this with service classes. If you have an OrderService and create a CachedOrderService that extends it, but the cached version skips saving to the database, any code expecting OrderService will think orders are persisted when they're not. The fix is usually to avoid inheritance and use interfaces or composition instead. So for Square and Rectangle, you'd have both implement a Shape interface independently rather than one extending the other.

sections.title: Fixing LSP Violations Through Design
sections.content:
When you discover an LSP violation, the fix is rarely "make the subclass behave exactly like the parent" — that's often impossible. Instead, you **restructure the inheritance**. The most common solution is replacing inheritance with a **common interface** that both classes implement independently, without shared mutable state. Another approach is **composition** — instead of a subclass extending a parent, the subclass contains an instance of the parent and delegates selectively.

In Spring Boot, this appears frequently: instead of CachedOrderService extends OrderService, you'd have both implement OrderService interface, and CachedOrderService uses composition by holding a DatabaseOrderService instance.

The key insight: inheritance should only be used when the subclass truly is a behavioral replacement, not just a conceptual category match.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Spot It|~broken contract|subclass throws or no-ops|behaves unlike the base
blue|Fix 1|~rethink hierarchy|extract a common base|Square and Rectangle → Shape
emerald|Fix 2|~composition|hold the behavior, don't inherit it
violet|Fix 3|~segregate|capability interfaces (ties to ISP)

sections.title: Fixing Rectangle-Square with Interface
When to Apply Each Fix
sections.content:
Use the **interface approach** when subclasses have fundamentally different state or invariants — Rectangle has two independent dimensions, Square has one constrained dimension, so shared setters make no sense.

Use **composition** when you want to reuse some parent behavior but need to override or skip parts — a CachingUserService can compose a DatabaseUserService and call it only on cache misses.

Use **strategy pattern** when behavior varies at runtime — instead of inheritance for different payment types, inject a PaymentStrategy. In Spring Boot, favor **dependency injection of interfaces** over extending concrete service classes. If you find yourself adding throws UnsupportedOperationException to overridden methods, that's a signal you need one of these fixes, not inheritance.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Throwing UnsupportedOperationException**: Freshers think overriding a method to throw this exception is a valid fix — it's actually another LSP violation because callers still break at runtime.
- **Abstract parent class with no-op methods**: Creating an abstract base class where some methods do nothing, then making subclasses override them — this just moves the LSP violation around.
- **Keeping inheritance and documenting restrictions**: Adding JavaDoc that says "don't call setHeight on Square" is not a fix — code shouldn't rely on documentation to avoid crashes.
- **Over-engineering with interfaces**: Creating an interface with 20 methods when inheritance would work fine — LSP violations only matter when the subclass actually breaks substitution.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Interface over inheritance**: extract common interface when subclass cannot honor parent contract
**Composition over inheritance**: hold parent instance instead of extending it
**Eliminate shared mutable state**: if subclass must enforce invariants parent doesn't, separate them
**Strategy pattern**: replace inheritance hierarchy with injected behavior objects
**No UnsupportedOperationException**: throwing this in overridden methods is an LSP violation itself
**Favor immutability**: records and immutable classes naturally avoid many LSP pitfalls
**Test substitutability**: write unit tests that use parent type and run with all subclass instances

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When you find an LSP violation, the fix is usually to stop using inheritance. The best approach is extracting a common interface that both classes implement independently. Take the Rectangle and Square problem. Instead of Square extending Rectangle, you'd create a Shape interface with methods like getArea and getPerimeter. Then Rectangle and Square both implement Shape, but they have their own separate state — Rectangle has width and height fields, Square has a single side field. Neither is trying to pretend to be the other. Another common fix is composition. Let's say you have an OrderService and you want a cached version. Instead of CachedOrderService extends OrderService, you'd make both implement an OrderService interface, and CachedOrderService holds a DatabaseOrderService instance inside. It calls the database service only when the cache misses. One thing freshers often do wrong is throwing UnsupportedOperationException in an overridden method. That's not a fix — it's still an LSP violation because callers crash at runtime. If you're adding that exception, it's a sign you shouldn't be using inheritance at all. The general principle is favor composition over inheritance. Inheritance should only be used when the subclass truly can substitute for the parent in every scenario.

title: UnsupportedOperationException and LSP violation
direct_answer: Throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass method is an LSP violation. It means the subclass cannot fulfill the contract of the parent — code that calls that method on the parent type will break at runtime when given the subclass. A real-world example is Collections.unmodifiableList() — calling add() throws, which surprises callers.

sections.title: Why UnsupportedOperationException Violates LSP
sections.content:
When a subclass overrides a method and throws **UnsupportedOperationException**, it's declaring "I cannot do what my parent promised." This is a textbook **LSP violation** because callers using the parent type expect the method to work. The compiler allows it because UnsupportedOperationException is a **runtime exception** (unchecked), so there's no compile-time error.

But at runtime, code crashes unexpectedly. The Java Collections Framework has famous examples: Collections.unmodifiableList() returns a List that throws UnsupportedOperationException on add(), remove(), and clear(). While pragmatic for immutability, this technically violates LSP — code expecting a List can call add() and will crash. Freshers often use this pattern when extending abstract classes, thinking it's a valid way to "disable" methods, but it's actually admitting the inheritance is wrong.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The Red Flag|~opting out|subclass can't honor a method|throws UnsupportedOperationException
blue|Why It Breaks LSP|~caller surprise|the base promised it works|the subtype refuses at runtime
emerald|Real Example|~immutable List|List.of().add() throws|substitution unsafe
violet|The Fix|~split the interface|MutableList vs ReadOnlyList

sections.title: UnsupportedOperationException LSP Violation
When This Pattern Appears
sections.content: You'll encounter UnsupportedOperationException violations in **legacy code** where inheritance was misused and fixing it would break too much. The **Java Collections API** uses it for unmodifiable wrappers as a pragmatic trade-off — immutability is valuable enough to accept the LSP violation. It also appears in **abstract base classes** where the designer wanted a "template" with some methods optional, but Spring Boot's design discourages this — use interfaces with default methods instead. In **repository patterns**, freshers sometimes create a ReadOnlyRepository extending a full repository and throw UnsupportedOperationException on write methods. This is wrong — the read-only version should be a separate interface. If you're tempted to use this pattern, it's a code smell that your inheritance hierarchy is incorrect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking it's a valid way to disable methods**: Freshers see abstract base classes with 10 methods, only need 5, so override the rest to throw UnsupportedOperationException — this just documents that inheritance is wrong.
- **Relying on documentation**: Adding JavaDoc like "don't call add() on this list" doesn't prevent runtime crashes — callers using the interface won't see that documentation.
- **Believing unchecked exceptions are safe**: Because UnsupportedOperationException is a runtime exception, freshers think it won't break callers — but any exception breaks callers, checked or not.
- **Not considering testing implications**: Unit tests that use the parent type will fail intermittently when a subclass is substituted, making the codebase fragile.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Runtime exception doesn't make it OK**: UnsupportedOperationException being unchecked means no compile error, but callers still crash
**Contract violation**: if parent interface declares a method, all implementations must honor it
**Collections API trade-off**: Java uses this for unmodifiable collections as pragmatic immutability, despite LSP violation
**Signal of wrong inheritance**: if you're throwing this, you probably shouldn't be using inheritance
**Testing reveals it**: substitutability tests (parent type, subclass instances) will catch these violations
**Better alternatives**: separate interfaces, composition, or strategy pattern avoid this issue
**Documentation is not a fix**: JavaDoc warnings don't prevent runtime crashes

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass method is an LSP violation. It means the subclass can't do what the parent promised, so code using the parent type will crash at runtime. The classic example is Java's Collections API. If you call Collections.unmodifiableList on an ArrayList, you get back a List reference. But if you try to call add on it, you get UnsupportedOperationException. Code that expects a List thinks add should work, so this is technically an LSP violation. Java makes this trade-off for immutability — it's pragmatic but not theoretically clean. Freshers often use this pattern when extending a base class. Let's say you have a UserRepository with save, delete, and findById methods, and you want a read-only version. A common mistake is creating ReadOnlyUserRepository that extends UserRepository and overrides save and delete to throw UnsupportedOperationException. This seems logical, but it violates LSP because callers expecting UserRepository will crash when they try to save. The right fix is separate interfaces — a ReadRepository with just read methods, and a WriteRepository with write methods. Then your read-only implementation only implements ReadRepository. If you find yourself throwing UnsupportedOperationException, it's a strong signal that inheritance is the wrong tool and you should be using interfaces or composition instead.

beats.content: When a class implements an interface, it's making a behavioral promise. The interface says: give me X, I'll give you back Y. An implementation that returns null, swallows the call silently, or throws unexpectedly breaks that promise, even if the code compiles perfectly.

A List implementation whose add() does nothing is an LSP violation. Callers expect the item to be there after the call. Getting surprised by an empty list is exactly the kind of behavioral mismatch LSP guards against.

non-obvious: the formal version of this is Design by Contract, where you document preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. In Java you don't always write contracts explicitly, but they exist implicitly in every interface. LSP says every implementation must honor those implicit contracts.

direct_answer: LSP is really about honoring contracts. When a class implements an interface, it promises to fulfill that contract. sections.title: LSP as Contract Fulfillment
sections.content:
LSP is fundamentally about **contracts** — not just type hierarchies. When a class implements an interface or extends a parent class, it's making a promise about behavior. The **interface contract** includes not just method signatures, but the expected behavior: what inputs are valid, what outputs are guaranteed, what exceptions can be thrown, and what side effects occur. If an implementation compiles but violates these expectations, it breaks LSP. This is formalized in **Design by Contract** (DbC), created by Bertrand Meyer. In DbC, every method has three parts: **preconditions** (what must be true before the method runs), **postconditions** (what the method guarantees after running), and **invariants** (properties that always hold). LSP requires subclasses to weaken or maintain preconditions, strengthen or maintain postconditions, and preserve all invariants.

In Spring Boot, think of it this way: if your PaymentService interface promises that processPayment returns a transaction ID and updates the order status, every implementation must do both — no silent failures, no skipped updates.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Contract = Behavior|~not just signatures|pre and postconditions count|exceptions are part of it
blue|Honor the Promise|~implementers|same guarantees as the type|no weaker behavior
emerald|LSP + Interfaces|~design by contract|callers trust the interface|every impl must keep it
violet|Break|~ignored contract|returns null where non-null promised

sections.title: Contract Violation Example
When Contract Thinking Matters
sections.content: Apply contract thinking when designing **Spring service interfaces**. If OrderService has a method placeOrder that returns an Order object, every implementation must return a fully initialized Order, not null or a partial object. In **repository interfaces**, the contract for save() is that the entity is persisted and returned with a generated ID — implementations can't silently skip the database write. For **validation**, if a method's precondition is that the input must not be null, subclasses cannot require additional constraints like "must be positive" — that would **strengthen the precondition**, violating LSP. Contract thinking is critical in **integration tests** — you should test behavior expectations, not just that methods don't throw exceptions. Write tests that verify postconditions: after calling processPayment, the order status must be updated.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking LSP is only about inheritance**: Freshers learn "subclass must replace parent" and miss that interface implementations have the same requirement — an implementation must honor the interface contract.
- **Ignoring implicit contracts**: Methods have behavioral expectations beyond the signature — a findById that returns null instead of throwing NoSuchElementException when the entity doesn't exist violates the implicit contract.
- **Strengthening preconditions**: Making a subclass require more validation than the parent — if parent accepts null, subclass cannot throw NullPointerException.
- **Weakening postconditions**: Returning less information than promised — if the contract says return a list of all matching items, returning the first 10 violates it.
- **Silent failures**: Methods that catch exceptions and return empty results instead of propagating errors — callers expecting exceptions for error handling are broken.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Preconditions**: subclass can accept more inputs than parent (weaken), never fewer (strengthen)
**Postconditions**: subclass must provide at least what parent promises (strengthen or maintain), never less
**Invariants**: properties that hold for parent must hold for subclass — no exceptions
**Exception contracts**: cannot throw new checked exceptions not in parent signature
**Implicit contracts**: behavior expectations beyond method signature matter — nullability, ordering, completeness
**Design by Contract**: formal framework for preconditions, postconditions, invariants from Bertrand Meyer
**Interfaces count**: LSP applies to interface implementations, not just class inheritance

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: LSP is really about honoring contracts, not just type compatibility. When a class implements an interface, it's making a promise about behavior. That promise includes preconditions, postconditions, and invariants — not just the method signature. Preconditions are what must be true before the method runs. Postconditions are what the method guarantees after it finishes. Invariants are properties that always hold. LSP says a subclass or implementation must maintain or weaken preconditions, maintain or strengthen postconditions, and always preserve invariants. Here's a concrete example. Say you have a PaymentService interface with a processPayment method. The contract says it returns a transaction ID and updates the order status to PAID. If you create a MockPaymentService for testing that just returns null and doesn't update the order status, you've violated the contract even though the code compiles. Callers expect that transaction ID and status update. This applies to interfaces just as much as class inheritance. Freshers sometimes think LSP is only about subclassing, but it's really about any substitution. If you promise a behavior, you have to deliver it. One way to think about this is implicit vs explicit contracts. The method signature is the explicit contract. But there are implicit contracts too — like findById should return null or throw an exception if the entity doesn't exist, not return a partial object. Design by Contract is the formal version of this idea, with explicit preconditions and postconditions.

sections.title: Structural vs Behavioral Relationships
sections.content:
In object-oriented programming, there's a critical distinction between **is-a** and **behaves-like-a**. The **is-a relationship** is about taxonomy or classification — it's what you'd find in a dictionary or biology textbook. A square is a rectangle in mathematics. A penguin is a bird in zoology. But **behaves-like-a** is about **substitutability** — can you use one thing everywhere you use another without breaking anything? This is what LSP demands. In OOP, inheritance should be based on behaves-like-a, not is-a. The classic trap: a square is a rectangle mathematically, so freshers make Square extend Rectangle. But a Square doesn't behave like a Rectangle in code — it can't have independent width and height, which Rectangle's contract allows.

The real-world taxonomy doesn't translate to OOP behavior.

In Spring Boot, this shows up when modeling domains: an AdminUser might be a User taxonomically, but if admin users have different authentication, permissions, and audit requirements, the behavioral contract is different and inheritance is wrong.

sections.content:
amber|IS-A|~structural|Square is-a Rectangle (math)|name and shape match only
blue|BEHAVES-LIKE-A|~behavioral|must act like the base everywhere|the real LSP test
emerald|Why It Matters|~is-a can lie|Penguin is-a Bird but can't fly()
violet|Rule|~inherit on behavior|if behaves-like-a fails → compose

rows: Square doesn't behave-like-a Rectangle in code

sections.title: When to Apply Each Concept
sections.content:
Use **is-a thinking** for domain modeling and documentation — understanding that a SavingsAccount is-a BankAccount helps you organize concepts and name classes clearly. But use **behaves-like-a thinking** for actual inheritance decisions. Before making class B extend class A, ask: "Can B be used everywhere A is used without surprises?" In Spring Boot **entity modeling**, an Employee might is-a Person taxonomically, but if Employee has required fields like employeeId and department that Person doesn't, and code operates on Person objects assuming those fields are absent, inheritance breaks.

Use **composition instead** — Employee has-a Person. For **service classes**, if you're creating specialized services, check behavioral compatibility: does CachedOrderService truly behave like OrderService in every scenario, or does it skip database writes? If it skips, don't inherit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Modeling the real world directly**: Freshers learn domain concepts like "a car is a vehicle" and immediately create class Car extends Vehicle, without checking if the code actually needs that relationship or if behavioral contracts match.
- **Inheritance for code reuse**: Using inheritance just to reuse methods — "User has a login method, so AdminUser should extend User to get it" — even when admin login behavior is different, violating LSP.
- **Biology and math as OOP rules**: Thinking "a penguin is a bird, and birds fly, so penguin should inherit fly method" — then overriding fly to do nothing or throw an exception, which is an LSP violation.
- **Ignoring invariants**: Employee is-a Person, so extending Person seems right, but if Person has an invariant that SSN is optional and Employee requires it, the invariant is broken.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **is-a is taxonomy**: real-world classification, useful for understanding domains
**behaves-like-a is LSP**: substitutability, determines valid inheritance
**Inheritance requires behavioral match**: not just conceptual category membership
**Real-world doesn't map to code**: mathematical or biological is-a doesn't guarantee OOP is-a
**Composition over inheritance**: when is-a holds but behaves-like-a doesn't, use has-a
**Behavioral contracts dominate**: method expectations, side effects, invariants matter more than domain vocabulary
**Penguin-Bird problem**: classic example where taxonomy (is-a) conflicts with behavior (fly method)

sections.content: is-a and behaves-like-a are two different kinds of relationships, and understanding the difference is key to using inheritance correctly. is-a is a taxonomic or classification relationship. It's what you'd find in a dictionary. A square is a rectangle in math. A penguin is a bird in biology. That's is-a. But behaves-like-a is about substitutability. Can you use one thing everywhere you use another without breaking anything? That's the LSP requirement. In object-oriented programming, inheritance should be based on behaves-like-a, not is-a. Here's why this matters. A square is a rectangle taxonomically, so it seems natural to write class Square extends Rectangle. But a rectangle lets you set width and height independently. A square enforces that both are equal. So a square doesn't behave like a rectangle from the code's perspective. If you pass a Square to a method expecting a Rectangle, the method might set width to five and height to four, expecting an area of twenty. But it gets sixteen instead because the Square changed both dimensions. That's a behavior mismatch. Another example: a penguin is a bird, but if your Bird class has a fly method, a penguin can't fulfill that contract. Overriding fly to do nothing or throw an exception is an LSP violation. The real-world taxonomy doesn't translate to code behavior. The key insight is that OOP inheritance should be driven by behavioral contracts, not domain vocabulary. If the behaviors don't match, use composition instead. A penguin can have a bird instance inside it, or both can implement a common Animal interface.
